URL: https://www.iranintl.com/en/202611200129
Iran International, 20 November 2026

Judge Mohammad Bemani, who heads Branch 2 of Yazd’s Revolutionary Court, issued the sentence in a joint case known as the “Yazd telecommunications” case, according to information received by Iran International and the rights group HRANA.

Three other men in the case, Mehdi Rajabi, Mohammad Kargar and Mohini Makki, were each sentenced to 20 years, to be served in internal exile in the prison of Zahedan, in Sistan and Baluchestan province, more than 800 kilometers away.

The charge announced was “taking part in setting fire to public property.” The details of the accusations against the men are not known, and it is not clear whether Fakhrabadi has appealed.

The case stems from protests on January 8 and 9, the days of the January massacre, when Imam Hossein Square in Yazd was one of the city’s main protest sites. The telecommunications building on the square and other government offices nearby, including one belonging to the Imam Khomeini Relief Committee, a state welfare foundation, caught fire.

100%Pouya Fakhrabadi$RS("S:a","P:a")‘They broke his head with a rifle butt’$RS("S:b","P:b")Fakhrabadi, who holds a master’s degree in physical education, was arrested at his home in Yazd on February 20, a source familiar with the case told Iran International. Security agents broke his head with a rifle butt during the raid, leaving a wound that needed 20 stitches, the source said.

In solitary confinement he was severely beaten and tortured and lost about 30 kilograms, the source said. Agents forced him to confess by threatening to kill members of his family and to sexually abuse them. He was denied a lawyer throughout the case.

His sister, who saw the violence during his arrest, suffered severe panic attacks and could barely speak for months afterward, the source said.

Fakhrabadi is a champion in hanmadang, the taekwondo discipline of creative and power breaking. He won gold at the international Kukkiwon Cup, organized by the sport’s world headquarters in South Korea, and has won a national title, setting a new record.

Of 28 people from the January protests held in Yazd prison, 15 have been sentenced to between three and 21 years, and 13 are still awaiting a verdict, HRANA reported on Tuesday.

In the months since the protests, Iran’s judiciary has handed down death sentences, prison terms, floggings and asset confiscations to many of those detained and to other political prisoners.

On Wednesday, the UN General Assembly’s human rights committee adopted a draft resolution condemning the crackdown on the January protests and calling for a halt to all executions, with a view to abolishing the death penalty.

In Isfahan, prosecutors have extended the detention of human rights lawyer Amirsalar Davoudi by 30 days and added a new charge, his lawyer, Mehdi Karimi Farsi, told the Emtedad news site.

Davoudi, who was sentenced in 2019 to 30 years in prison and 111 lashes over his work defending political prisoners, was arrested again on October 11. He already faced charges of “spreading falsehoods online,” “propaganda against the system” and “inciting people to war and killing each other to disrupt national security.” He now also faces “producing and spreading false news against national security in wartime.”

Moein Khazaeli, a lawyer, wrote on X that prosecutors brought the new charge under Article 4 of a law toughening penalties for espionage, passed after the June 2025 war. It carries 10 to 15 years in prison, he said, or death if the court treats it as “corruption on earth.” He said the law was being used to stop lawyers defending their clients.

Part of the case against Davoudi stems from a recording he posted on Instagram on October 4 of a wedding ceremony conducted by phone between two of his imprisoned clients, Mahshad Keshani and Alireza Sepahi Badjani. Sepahi Badjani was executed the next day.

Davoudi suffered a heart attack in solitary confinement on November 8 and was taken to Isfahan’s Al-Zahra hospital, Iran Human Rights reported. The next morning, he was taken to court to be charged. He has had no contact with his family since his arrest, his lawyer said, despite a court order on November 15 allowing calls.

UN human rights experts said on November 9 that Davoudi’s arrest was part of a campaign of pressure on independent lawyers, at least 135 of whom faced judicial or security action in Iran between September 2025 and September 2026.

"])•••$RC("B:5","S:5")More StoriesHundreds of writers urge Iran to halt poet's executionNov 19, 2026, 09:27 GMT+0Listen to this article100%Peyman Farahavar, an Iranian poet sentenced to death on charges of armed rebellion and waging war against God.Hundreds of poets and prominent literary figures worldwide have joined an international campaign calling on Iran to halt the execution of imprisoned poet Peyman Farahavar, whose death sentence has been upheld and referred for enforcement.

“Nowhere in the world should words and poetry be punishable by hanging,” the signatories said in a joint statement urging international action to save his life.

Among those backing the campaign are Goncourt Prize winners Leila Slimani and Marie NDiaye, International Booker Prize winner David Diop, American poet Charles Bernstein and French writer Daniel Pennac.

Iranian poets and writers, including Hafez Mousavi, Fatemeh Ekhtesari, Fatemeh Shams, Mehdi Moosavi and Ziba Karbassi, also signed the appeal.

The Writers' Association of Iran announced on November 15 that Farahavar's death sentence on charges of baghi (armed rebellion) and moharebeh (waging war against God) had been finalized.

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi said the same day that his case had been referred to the sentence enforcement department.

Human rights news agency HRANA reported on November 11, citing a source close to Farahavar's family, that he had informed relatives by telephone on November 9 that he had received official notification that his death sentence had been referred for enforcement.

100%Peyman Farahavar, an Iranian poet sentenced to death on charges of armed rebellion and waging war against God.Farahavar was sentenced to death in May 2025 by Branch One of the Revolutionary Court in Rasht. The Supreme Court upheld the sentence later that year and rejected his request for a retrial in April 2026.

Writers denounce forced confessions

Farahavar was arrested in 2022 over protest poetry, videos of poetry readings shared online and a solitary street demonstration, according to the campaign statement.

“His initial trial was conducted without a lawyer, and confessions extracted under duress formed the basis of his death sentence,” the signatories said.

The writers described the sentence as “manifestly unjust and contrary to recognized human rights standards and the principles of a fair trial.”

The statement also highlighted broader concerns about executions in Iran, particularly those involving protesters and people prosecuted for exercising freedom of expression.

“We, the poets signing this letter, call on the Iranian public, the media and international organizations, in the name of freedom and justice, to use every means at their disposal to compel the authorities of the Islamic Republic to immediately halt Peyman Farahavar's execution,” the statement said.

The Writers' Association of Iran also said at least 20 writers and poets were serving prison sentences or being held in prolonged detention, with several facing serious charges.

The campaign called for an end to death sentences imposed for peaceful expression, warning that Farahavar's case reflected wider concerns over the treatment of writers and dissenting voices in Iran.

Listen to this article100%Family members dance beside the grave of Alireza Raeisi, a 21-year-old Iranian protester executed on October 5, 2026, in connection with the January protests in Isfahan.Iranian families are turning funerals for slain protesters into acts of defiance, using music and dance to challenge the Islamic Republic's use of mourning rituals and symbols to reinforce its authority.

A father and mother dance in the center as crowds cheer and clap to upbeat music. They are outside, surrounded by bouquets of colorful flowers and white doves. From a distance, the scene could easily be mistaken for a wedding or a birthday celebration. But it is neither. It is a funeral, taking place at the grave of their child, who was killed in the Islamic Republic's crackdown on protesters.

This seeming contradiction gives the scene its political force: while the family grieves, they refuse to do so in the language of mourning expected by the country's religious and political establishment.

“This cheering [at the grave] is not mourning; it is a ritual of revenge.”

That line, written by Iranian songwriter Mona Borzouee and performed by legendary Iranian pop star Ebi, speaks directly to the scene captured in a video circulating online.

The song and music video “Bego be Donya” (“Tell the World”) mourn the thousands of Iranian protesters killed during the January 2026 protests. But throughout the song, mourning is not simply an expression of sadness. It becomes memory, anger and, most importantly, resistance.

The song evokes images of the dead, grieving parents, graves and dancing bodies, transforming personal loss into a public act that demands to be seen and remembered. Parents confront the unbearable pain of losing a child, refusing to let death have the final word.

At funerals and 40-day memorials for protesters killed in the streets, families have begun dancing, playing music, clapping, reading poetry and celebrating the lives of their children rather than expressing grief through traditional Islamic mourning rituals.

One of the most powerful expressions of this shift came from Majid-Reza Rahnavard, a 23-year-old Iranian protester detained during the 2022 protests and subsequently executed by the Islamic Republic.

Surrounded by masked guards and blindfolded, Rahnavard appeared on state television shortly before his execution. His final words were: “I don't want anyone to mourn upon my grave. I don't want them to read the Quran or pray. Just celebrate and play celebrating, happy music.”

Rahnavard's words challenged the symbolic structure of official mourning. Through music, dance and celebration, grieving families affirm the lives of their loved ones.

In this context, the phrase “a ritual of revenge” carries a deeper symbolic and political meaning: refusing to submit, preserving the memory of the dead and continuing to live despite the government's attempts to instill fear and silence.
